IEE Colloquium onDigital Signal Processing and Display Techniques for Ultrasonics
abstract: Summary form only given. The work at Southampton General Hospital has concentrated on developing the broadband ultrasonic attenuation technique for both the absolute assessment and longitudinal monitoring of the effects of osteoporosis. Initial work involving a single site quantitative measurement has indicated the need to improve reproducibility. To address this problem an imaging system has been developed to accurately locate recognisable anatomical sites and hence base consecutive measurements on the same region of bone. To investigate the resolution that might be attainable with this technique images of the os calcis have been acquired at frequencies of 200, 400 and 600 kHz using both focussed and non-focussed probes. In vitro phantom measurements have also been carried out to assess the performance of these probes and to compare them with the vivo assessment.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium onDigital Signal Processing and Display Techniques for Ultrasonics
abstract: Summary form only give, as follows. The data processing aspects of ultrasonic NDT are reviewed mainly with respect to work carried out recently at Harwell. The objective is to show how increasingly sophisticated methods of data processing, such as SAFT, image sharpening, pattern recognition, etc., are beginning to be applied. They can lead to more objective decision on behalf of the inspector and greater reliability. These methods however required extensive data and this leads to potential problems in data storage and computer speed. The extend of this problem is illustrated with simple examples. Computer performance will continue to increase so that brute force solutions to this problem are probable eventually. However it is worth looking at ways to avoid having to use ever larger computer power.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium onDigital Signal Processing and Display Techniques for Ultrasonics
abstract: Summary form only given, as follows. Objective computer-based analysis methods are described for reliably distinguishing significant defects such as cracks from more benign indications arising from volumetric flaws such as slag and porosity. The methods are based firstly on colour imaging techniques which are used to display 3-D ultrasonic data obtained from defects scanned using multiple inspection techniques. The resultant images give an invaluable qualitative guide to defect type and facilitate the derivation of numerical descriptors or 'features' based on well-defined physical principles. Statistical pattern recognition methods are then used for defect classification, by analysis of the feature values obtained from scanning many known examples of each defect type.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Application of digital ultrasonics to the testing of shaft forgings
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium onDigital Signal Processing and Display Techniques for Ultrasonics
abstract: Summary form only given. In-service ultrasonic flaw detection by the A-scan technique is carried out by British coal on a variety of shaft forgings of lengths up to 9 metres. An insight is given into the problems associated with the testing of shaft forgings and the developments that have taken place within British Coal are discussed. Future developments, based upon current experience in the use of digital ultrasonics, which are required to improve further the reliability of testing, are also discussed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: The analysis of speckle and texture in medical ultrasonics
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium onDigital Signal Processing and Display Techniques for Ultrasonics
abstract: A basic assumption of 'ultrasonic tissue characterization' is that quantitation of the interactions between ultrasound and tissue will provide information which is more tissue specific than that obtained by current visual observation of pulse-echo images. Many approaches to this goal are being assessed; for example the measurement of propagation properties such as ultrasound speed, attenuation coefficient or nonlinearity parameter. In their laboratory the authors have tended to concentrate on quantifying tissue characteristics which are associated with morphology rather than chemical composition, as assessed by the ultrasound scattering-related properties of tissues. Some of the methods which they have developed, particularly those which they feel have potential for clinical application are described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Digital analysis techniques and signal processing at Keele (University)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium onDigital Signal Processing and Display Techniques for Ultrasonics
abstract: Gives an introduction to the Ultrasonics and Digital Signal Processing (UDSP) Laboratory at the University of Keele and summarises the main research activities currently in progress. Research into the ultrasonic properties of adhesive materials and adhesively bonded structures is also described in greater detail.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium onDigital Signal Processing and Display Techniques for Ultrasonics
abstract: The 1-D born Inversion technique is well established as a method which gives defect radii from pulse-echo ultrasonic measurements. Recent developments have provided a robust sizing technique for weak scatterers that gives the diameter of a flaw from measurements in the Born Radius/Zero-of-Time Shift Domain (BR/ZOTSD) without the explicit need to select a correct zero-of-time for the inversion. The paper reports some aspects of the extension of this work to consider the sizing of strong scatterers such as spherical voids and inclusions.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Computer graphics for ultrasonic data interpretation
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium onDigital Signal Processing and Display Techniques for Ultrasonics
abstract: Highly automated ultrasonic inspection systems under computer control are used in some cases where the cost of plant is high and the consequences of failure unacceptable. These inspection systems generate large quantities of data. To aid the ultrasonic engineer in the task of assessing such data the authors are developing a computer graphics system to enhance his productivity and help with the 'housekeeping'. They have called it GUIDE (Graphical Ultrasonic Inspection Data Evaluation). A prototype of the system has been developed, as part of the design process, and is in use in the CEGB NDT Applications Centre.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Digital techniques in laser generated ultrasound
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium onDigital Signal Processing and Display Techniques for Ultrasonics
abstract: Summary form only given. The authors have used three types of noncontacting receiver and evaluated their performance-capacitance transducers, electromagnetic acoustic transducers and laser interferometers. All have their advantages and can be readily interfaced to a digitisation system. The various digitisation techniques that they have used including Tektronix, LeCroy and Gould systems are discussed and a system that would be suitable to be used with an industrial version of this remote technique is defined. In addition they describe the various analytical facilities that are available with digitised data. The application of the laser technique to the study of delaminations in carbon fibre material and debonds in plasma sprayed material illustrates the display techniques that can be linked to a scanning laser system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium onDigital Signal Processing and Display Techniques for Ultrasonics
abstract: Automated high sensitivity ultrasonic inspections of thick-section weldments using multi-probe arrays are increasingly being used as a reliable method of defect detection. Very large amounts of data are often collected, much of which is not associated with defect signals but with cladding noise, geometrical reflections, probe reverberations or electronic noise. The noise signals are often of higher amplitude than signals from real defects and cannot therefore be eliminated by simply raising the recording threshold. The reliability and speed of the analysis of this type of data is difficult and is still dependent on the operator. Developments aimed at automating the defect detection process are described.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
